title: B2B LinkedIn Ads Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how well your targeting, creative, landing pages, and lead handling work together to drive consistent B2B growth from LinkedIn.

low.headline: Fix the foundation before you scale the spend
low.text: The basics matter more than people think. A broken company page link, a sparse profile, or an unreviewed account setup quietly undermines every ad you run — the moment someone clicks through, trust is already at stake. These are fast fixes with immediate payback.
steps: Test the link between your ad account and company page — click through yourself and see what a prospect actually lands on
Update your company page: logo, banner, clear description, website link, and at least a few recent posts
Do a full review of your ad account setup including tracking, permissions, and billing — small gaps compound

mid.headline: Good start — close the gaps before they cost you
mid.text: The basics are mostly in place, but there are probably things that haven't been looked at in a while. Small oversights at the foundation level have a way of costing more than they should.
steps: Verify the company page connection is working correctly — click through from an active ad and confirm where it lands
Set a quarterly review of your company page and account setup so nothing drifts
Make sure your LinkedIn presence reflects what a prospect would expect after seeing your ad

high.headline: Solid foundation — now make sure it's working for you
high.text: You've got the housekeeping sorted. The next question is whether your setup is actively building trust with prospects or just not getting in the way.
steps: Look at your company page with fresh eyes — does it build confidence for someone who's never heard of you?
Keep the review cadence consistent so nothing quietly breaks between campaigns
Treat your LinkedIn company page as a trust signal, not just a technical requirement

low.headline: Targeting is the fastest lever you can pull right now
low.text: If you're not clear on who you're reaching, everything else — creative, messaging, landing pages, lead handling — becomes guesswork. Nailing targeting is the first step to making LinkedIn Ads worth the spend.
steps: Define your ideal customer specifically: job title, seniority, company size, and industry — not just a general description
Research what your competitors are running in LinkedIn Ads before you write a word of ad copy — gaps in their messaging are often your best opportunities
Set a monthly review of audience performance data so you can cut what isn't working and put more behind what is

mid.headline: You're pointed in the right direction — sharpen it
mid.text: You have a working picture of who you're going after. The gap is usually in how often you revisit it and how much you know about what's working in your space right now.
steps: Use LinkedIn's audience insights to check whether the people actually engaging match who you thought you were targeting
Do a competitor ad review this quarter — it takes a couple of hours and the gaps you find are often directly usable
Test a tighter audience segment alongside your current one and let the data tell you which performs better

high.headline: Strong targeting practice — keep the loop tight
high.text: You're doing the things that make targeting compound over time. The risk at this stage is assuming what worked last quarter still holds — markets shift, and so does your competition.
steps: Keep running regular competitor checks — what's working for them today is data you can act on now
Document your targeting decisions so you can track what changed, when, and why
Test new audience segments as you grow — don't let a working setup turn into a stale one

low.headline: Weak creative and messaging costs you leads every day
low.text: Ads that say the wrong thing to the right people don't convert. Before you increase spend, get the message right. That starts with real buyer language — not what you think they want to hear.
steps: Pull your last 5–10 sales conversations and find the exact words your buyers use to describe their problems — that's your ad copy
Run at least two messaging angles at the same time so you have data to make decisions with, not just opinions
Set a four-week creative performance review as a non-negotiable — ad fatigue kills results quietly and quickly

mid.headline: Good instincts — build a proper test and refresh process
mid.text: You've got messaging that works well enough. The problem is that 'well enough' erodes over time, and ad hoc testing rarely catches it before performance drops.
steps: Move from occasional testing to always running at least two creative variants — the comparison is where the learning happens
Build a refresh schedule before performance drops, not after — proactive beats reactive every time
Check whether your call to action fits where the buyer actually is — someone who's never heard of you needs a different ask than a warm lead

high.headline: Strong creative discipline — now tighten the buyer journey match
high.text: You're running creative the right way. The next lever is usually in how precisely your ask maps to each stage of the buyer journey.
steps: Review whether each audience segment has creative designed specifically for them — a single message is a missed opportunity
Look at which calls to action have the best downstream conversion rate, not just the best click-through rate
Keep testing — what's converting now won't always convert

low.headline: Leads are falling through the cracks after the click
low.text: The ad is only half the job. What happens after someone clicks — the landing page they see, the follow-up they get, and what you do if they don't convert immediately — is where most of the money is lost. Fix this before increasing spend.
steps: Check whether your landing page continues the conversation the ad started — if the message changes between the ad and the page, you're losing people right there
Set up a clear, fast follow-up process for every lead that converts — the longer you wait, the colder they get
Build even a basic retargeting sequence for leads who didn't convert straight away — most B2B buyers need more than one touch before they're ready

mid.headline: The basics are there — close the gaps in follow-up
mid.text: You're not losing everything after the click, but there are gaps in how consistently leads get followed up with and what happens to the ones who don't convert immediately.
steps: Document your lead follow-up process so it doesn't depend on bandwidth or memory
Audit the message match between your ads and landing pages — even small inconsistencies reduce conversion rates
Set up retargeting for unconverted leads if you haven't already — it's often the highest-ROI addition you can make to an existing campaign

high.headline: You're thinking beyond the ad — that's what makes results sustainable
high.text: Most people focus on the ad and ignore what comes after. You're not doing that, and it's why your campaigns have a better chance of building on each other over time.
steps: Keep reviewing landing page message match as you introduce new creative — it drifts if you're not watching it
Track lead response time and downstream conversion rate by source to see where the follow-up process breaks down
Test different nurture approaches for unconverted leads — some buyers take longer and the right sequence makes the difference

questions.text: What is your current monthly LinkedIn Ads budget?
questions.hint: At least $1,000/month is needed to generate meaningful data. Most B2B campaigns get reliable traction from $2,000–$5,000/month.

questions.text: How many qualified leads does LinkedIn Ads generate for you each month?
questions.hint: Count only leads you would actually follow up on — not all form fills or clicks.

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend managing LinkedIn Ads?
questions.hint: Include time checking dashboards, writing briefs, reviewing reports, and handling leads. Exclude time your agency spends.

questions.text: How do you measure whether your LinkedIn Ads are actually working?

answers.label: We track from click through to closed revenue — not just impressions, clicks, or leads
We track leads and cost per lead, and connect them to pipeline
We look at clicks, impressions, and leads but haven't tied them to revenue
We mostly rely on what LinkedIn's native dashboard shows us
We don't have proper tracking in place — we're going on gut feel

low.headline: Without measurement, you're spending blind
low.text: If you can't tell whether LinkedIn Ads are working, you can't improve them. Setting up basic tracking and a review cadence is a one-time investment that pays back every month you run campaigns.
steps: Set up conversion tracking in LinkedIn Campaign Manager and connect it to your CRM so leads are tied to specific campaigns
Pick three metrics you'll review every month: cost per lead, lead quality, and pipeline generated
Build a simple spend decision rule — what number tells you to scale, and what tells you to pull back?

mid.headline: Good data habits — connect the dots all the way to revenue
mid.text: You're tracking the right things at the top of the funnel. The next step is tying those numbers to what actually closes, so you're making spend decisions based on revenue, not just lead volume.
steps: Work with your sales team to track which LinkedIn leads progress through the pipeline and which go cold
Review performance monthly, not just quarterly — trends show up faster than most people expect
Build your spend decision rule around cost per qualified opportunity, not just cost per lead

high.headline: You're running LinkedIn Ads like a proper growth channel
high.text: You measure what matters and make decisions based on data. That's what separates B2B companies who get sustainable results from LinkedIn Ads from the ones who give up after three months.
steps: Keep the measurement loop tight as you scale — what you track at $2k/month needs to evolve at $10k/month
Document your review cadence and spend decision rules so they survive team changes
Use attribution data to push budget toward the campaigns and audiences that close, not just the ones that click
